contextWarmup.prompt: When you are studying for a difficult exam or working on a hard project, what is the best way to handle stress?

rules: Three-part phrasal verbs always consist of a verb, an adverb or particle, and a preposition, such as look forward to, put up with, or run out of.
The three elements cannot be separated, meaning the object must always come at the very end of the phrase.
When a verb follows the final preposition in a three-part phrasal verb, it must take the gerund (-ing) form.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often put an infinitive verb after a prepositional phrasal verb instead of the required gerund form.

content.passageTitle: Navigating University Life and Complex Conversations
paragraphs: Starting university life can be both exciting and overwhelming for young adults. Students often find themselves facing situations where they must learn to put up with difficult roommates, noisy study halls, and tight schedules. However, those who manage to get along with their peers usually experience a much smoother transition. Learning how to communicate effectively helps students avoid unnecessary stress and build strong support networks during their first academic year.

Academic success also depends on creative thinking and resourcefulness. When researchers run out of funding or face unexpected roadblocks, they need to come up with innovative solutions quickly. Instead of complaining, successful scholars often bite the bullet and work extra hours in the laboratory. Furthermore, discussing project goals with colleagues ensures that everyone can see eye to eye before submitting final research papers.

content.summary: Mastering three-part phrasal verbs and common idioms to make your academic and informal writing sound natural at the B1 CEFR level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Three-Part Phrasal Verb Structure
blueprintItems.example: We are looking forward to visiting the museum.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Inseparable Elements Rule
blueprintItems.formula: Verb + Particle + Preposition (Never separate these three parts)
blueprintItems.example: She puts up with the noise every single day.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Integrating Idiomatic Expressions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + Idiomatic Phrase + Contextual Detail
blueprintItems.example: During the meeting, Mark hit the nail on the head.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always follow three-part phrasal verbs ending in 'to' with a gerund (-ing) or a noun.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I am looking forward to meet you.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I am looking forward to meeting you.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'to' in these phrasal verbs functions as a preposition, requiring a noun or an -ing verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not separate the three parts of a three-part phrasal verb.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She ran out her coffee of.
mechanicsRules.why: The verb, particle, and preposition must remain together directly before the object.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize proper names, titles, and the first word of every sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: mark is looking forward to coming up with a new plan.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Mark is looking forward to coming up with a new plan.
mechanicsRules.why: Standard English capitalization rules apply to all writing forms.
